papers.title: Dynamic Contracting
papers.venue: Annual Review of Economics, forthcoming (working paper, August 2025)
papers.tldr: The survey of dynamic mechanism design by one of its architects. Its organizing result: the static Myerson distortion carries over verbatim except that the inverse hazard rate is multiplied by an impulse response measuring how much a later type still depends on the initial one - so distortions shrink exactly as fast as impulse responses decay, and vanish entirely after period 1 when types are independent and the agent has deep pockets. Sections 4-9 survey what breaks when those assumptions go, and Section 10 is an unusually explicit open-problems list, including that no fully canonical class of mechanisms is known under limited commitment.

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence for Auction Design
papers.tldr: Six model-free reinforcement-learning algorithms are set to bid against each other in pay-as-bid, generalized second-price and uniform-price multi-unit auctions. The efficiency ranking is robust - uniform price wins in every configuration - but the revenue ranking is not: with a mixed population of unequally competent learners pay-as-bid raises over twice what uniform price does at high supply, and that advantage disappears once all six bidders are the best algorithm (PPO), where generalized second-price leads instead. Simulated revenue rankings are therefore an artifact of how well the artificial bidders have learned.

papers.title: The Near-Optimality of Two-Part Tariffs for Nonlinear Pricing
papers.venue: Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper No. 2534, Yale University
papers.tldr: A two-part tariff - fixed fee plus a constant markup over production cost - guarantees a fraction m/(m+1)^(1+1/m) of the optimal nonlinear-pricing profit for every regular value distribution, where m is the elasticity of marginal cost. The bound is tight, rises to 1 as costs become more convex, and fails entirely without an elasticity floor or under non-regularity, where a menu with one entry per ironing interval restores it. This is the quantitative foundation for cost-plus-fixed-fee procurement contracts, and it selects the same markup the prior-free literature does.

papers.title: Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control
papers.tldr: Because AI capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited, screening agents of unknown alignment and unknown capability admits a revelation principle - with incentive compatibility deterring double deviations, misreport then disobey - and a tight nested cyclical-monotonicity characterization that generalizes Rochet to unordered types and incomplete report graphs. Evaluations attain the full-information payoff when bias falls with capability and are worthless when it rises; alignment and interpretability are substitutes in the instrument but complements in value.

papers.title: Information Design for AI Proxies under Imperfect Recall
papers.tldr: A revelation principle survives imperfect recall: any outcome distribution achievable when the receiver must play one stationary response rule at every stage is achievable by a direct mechanism that simply recommends actions and in which obedience is optimal. Conditioning tomorrow's signal on today's realized action strictly expands the implementable set exactly when the agent reaches some outcome only after disobeying and is not indifferent over it.

papers.title: From Microeconomics to AI Research: A Guide for Economists
papers.tldr: A guide rather than a result: the RLHF pipeline is a stack of familiar microeconomic problems - reward modeling is exactly McFadden's conditional logit, aggregating annotators is social choice (and the standard estimator implicitly runs Borda), reward hacking is Holmstrom-Milgrom multitask moral hazard, sycophancy is a signaling game, and scaling laws behave like a Cobb-Douglas production function - plus a practical route into AI research for economists.

papers.title: Agentic Markets: Game Dynamics and Equilibrium in Markets with Learning Agents
papers.tldr: Agents running projected gradient ascent converge to a Nash equilibrium essentially only when that equilibrium is strict, and even then only locally: the paper's counterexample shows a unique strict equilibrium can fail to attract from a positive-measure set of initial conditions. Worse for economics, discretizing a well-behaved game such as Cournot oligopoly (needed because auctions have discontinuous payoffs) destroys the monotonicity and strictness on which every convergence guarantee rests.

papers.title: Information Design and Mechanism Design: An Integrated Framework
papers.venue: Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper 2494 / arXiv:2601.17267 (survey chapter)
papers.tldr: Written in quantile space, optimal screening and optimal information disclosure are the same problem: maximize a linear functional under a majorization constraint, solved by concavification. When a designer chooses both the allocation and the buyers' information, pooling is always optimal (Theorem 3), because pooling values raises payments at second order while the allocative distortion is only third order; in efficient auctions optimal disclosure is upper censorship that keeps roughly two bidders competing at the top regardless of N.

papers.title: From Conversations to Mechanisms: Aligning Advertiser Incentives in AI-Powered Product Recommendations
papers.venue: Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper No. 2513, Yale University
papers.tldr: Conditioning advertiser transfers on the user feedback that a multi-round AI shopping conversation generates — purchases, exits, follow-up queries — makes each advertiser residual claimant on realized social surplus and yields periodic ex-post implementation of the efficient recommendation policy, escaping the Jehiel et al. (2006) impossibility for multidimensional interdependent values without any external data. Participation and no-subsidy can each be secured by a pivotal Groves term, but jointly only when the platform's own data makes advertisers' private signals redundant.

papers.title: Menu Pricing of Large Language Models
papers.venue: Cowles Foundation Discussion Paper No. 2502 (also CEPR DP21275; TSE WP 1670; arXiv:2502.07736)
papers.tldr: Under a homogeneous inference technology, a user's infinite-dimensional profile of task values collapses to a scalar aggregate type and the hidden allocation of tokens across tasks adds no incentive constraints, so optimal LLM pricing reduces to one-dimensional Mussa-Rosen screening. The optimum is a menu of committed-spend contracts (an upfront fee for a budget spent on tokens priced at marginal cost), which rationalizes observed maximum-spend, minimum-spend and linear pay-per-token API pricing.

papers.title: Algorithmic Pricing and Algorithmic Collusion
papers.tldr: A BISE 'Catchword' overview arguing that algorithmic collusion is best understood as an instance of the unsolved learning-in-games problem: no-regret learners are only guaranteed to reach coarse correlated equilibrium, not Nash, and Bertrand competition falls outside the potential/monotone game classes where Nash convergence is known. It therefore remains unresolved whether observed supra-competitive prices reflect genuine tacit coordination or mere failure to converge -- which is exactly what antitrust policy would need to know.

papers.title: Procurement without Priors: A Simple Mechanism and its Notable Performance
papers.tldr: A buyer with no prior over supplier costs can still guarantee a constant fraction of first-best surplus by paying a fixed share of their own gross utility — and no mechanism, however complex, does better in the worst case.
